title: Intermittent auscultation and CTG interpretation
blurb: Listen in correctly with intermittent auscultation, categorise CTG features as white, amber or red, and act on the overall picture under NICE NG229.
question: Ruth, at 7 cm on continuous CTG because of meconium, has a baseline that has risen from 130 to 150 bpm over the last hour and variability of 4 bpm for 40 minutes. Contractions are 4 in 10 and there are no decelerations. How should the midwife categorise the trace, and what should she do?

teach.h: Listening to the baby in labour
teach.body: Formally: NICE NG229 recommends intermittent auscultation (IA) for women at low risk of complications, continuous cardiotocography (CTG) when antenatal or intrapartum risk factors are present, and categorisation of each CTG feature as white, amber or red to classify the trace as normal, suspicious or pathological. In plain English: listen regularly if all is well, monitor continuously if there are risks, and read the CTG as part of the whole clinical picture, not as a standalone test.

teach.caption: No fetal heartbeat detected: offer urgent real-time ultrasound (NG229 1.2.9).

steps.label: Baseline up 20+ bpm or a deceleration heard
Listen more often
steps.sub: e.g. after 3 consecutive contractions; full review

steps.label: Concern confirmed
steps.sub: summon help; advise continuous CTG; transfer if midwife-led

steps.label: CTG normal after 20 min
steps.sub: return to IA if no risk factors

head: Feature
White
Amber
Red
rows: Under 5 for 30–50 min; over 25 up to 10 min
Under 5 over 50 min; over 25 over 10 min; sinusoidal
Any late; prolonged 3 min+; bradycardia; concerning variable 30 min+ repetitive
teach.caption: NICE NG229 1.4.12–1.4.24 (late decelerations red since the 2025 amendment). Accelerations are reassuring; their absence alone does not mean acidosis.

items: Normal: continue CTG (unless started for IA concern with no risks) and hourly risk assessment.
Suspicious: full risk assessment and maternal observations, consider causes, conservative measures; urgent review if other risks (slow progress, sepsis, meconium).

Pathological: urgent obstetric AND senior midwife review; exclude acute events (cord prolapse, abruption, uterine rupture); conservative measures; if still pathological, further review and consider expediting birth.
Acute bradycardia or prolonged deceleration 3 min+: urgent obstetric review, prepare for urgent birth; expedite if it persists 9 minutes (sooner with risk factors).
Oxytocin running and CTG pathological: stop it immediately.

teach.body: Encourage mobilising or changing position and avoid lying supine. Do not give IV fluids for FHR abnormalities unless she is hypotensive or septic; for hypotension after an epidural top-up, give IV fluids, left lateral position and call the anaesthetist. Reduce or stop oxytocin and consider a tocolytic for excessive contractions. Do not give maternal facial oxygen. Each hourly CTG assessment needs an in-person 'fresh eyes' review by another clinician.

Contractions 4 in 10: white. Baseline risen by 20 bpm in the last hour: amber. Variability under 5 for 40 minutes: amber. No decelerations: white. Two amber features make the trace pathological. The midwife calls for urgent review by an obstetrician and a senior midwife, checks for acute events, does full maternal observations (looking for sepsis), starts conservative measures, explains to Ruth, and documents times. A falling variability with a rising baseline is a strong sign of compromise.

teach.text: Since the 2025 amendment, ANY late deceleration is a red feature, whatever its duration. And two amber features equal pathological, not 'very suspicious'. In the second stage, accelerations are most likely the maternal pulse.

items: IA: after a contraction, at least 1 minute, every 15 min (first stage) or every 5 min (second stage).
Rise of 20 bpm or a deceleration on IA: listen more often, full review; confirmed: CTG and transfer.
White, amber, red for contractions, baseline, variability, decelerations.
Normal all white; suspicious 1 amber; pathological 1 red or 2+ amber.
Pathological: urgent obstetric and senior midwife review; exclude acute events.
Bradycardia: expedite if persisting 9 minutes; no maternal facial oxygen; fresh eyes hourly.

summary: You can now perform intermittent auscultation correctly, escalate concerns, and categorise each CTG feature as white, amber or red. You can also classify a trace as normal, suspicious or pathological and take the actions NICE NG229 sets for each, including acute bradycardia.

A.q: How should intermittent auscultation be carried out for a low-risk woman in the established first stage of labour?
options: After a contraction, for 1 minute, every 15 minutes
During a contraction, for 30 seconds, every 15 minutes
After a contraction, for 1 minute, every 30 minutes
During a contraction, for 1 minute, every 5 minutes
A.why: NG229 1.2.9: immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, at least once every 15 minutes, recorded as a single rate.

whyNot.1: IA is done after the contraction, for at least 1 minute.
whyNot.3: Every 5 minutes is the second-stage interval, and IA follows the contraction.

A.q: A CTG has one amber feature and the other three are white. How should the trace be categorised?
options: Normal
Pathological
Abnormal
Suspicious
A.why: NG229 1.4.32: any 1 amber feature makes the trace suspicious.

whyNot.0: Normal requires all 4 features to be white.
whyNot.1: Pathological is any 1 red or 2 or more amber features.
whyNot.2: NG229 uses normal, suspicious and pathological.

A.q: How are late decelerations categorised on an intrapartum CTG under NICE NG229?
options: Amber if present for under 30 minutes
Red, at any duration
White if variability is normal
Amber if they are non-repetitive
A.why: NG229 1.4.24 (amended 2025): late decelerations are a red feature, irrespective of duration or repetition.

whyNot.0: The 30-minute rule applies to variable decelerations with concerning characteristics.
whyNot.2: Normal variability does not make late decelerations white.
whyNot.3: Late decelerations are red whether or not repetitive.

B.q: Neha is in the second stage of labour at a midwifery unit with intermittent auscultation. How should the midwife listen?
options: Every 15 minutes, palpating the maternal pulse
Every 5 minutes, palpating the pulse hourly
Every 5 minutes, palpating the maternal pulse
Continuously with a hand-held Doppler
B.why: NG229 1.2.10: in the second stage, auscultate after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, at least every 5 minutes, palpating the maternal pulse simultaneously.

whyNot.0: Every 15 minutes is the first-stage interval.
whyNot.1: The maternal pulse is palpated simultaneously each time in the second stage.
whyNot.3: Continuous hand-held Doppler is not the NG229 method.

B.q: On intermittent auscultation, Kate's fetal heart rate baseline has risen from 125 to 148 bpm since the start of labour. What should the midwife do?
options: Continue IA every 15 minutes as before
Listen more often and carry out a full review
Expedite the birth as an obstetric emergency
Give IV fluids and oxygen by face mask
B.why: NG229 1.2.11: a rise of 20 bpm or more from the start of labour means auscultating more often (for example after 3 consecutive contractions) and carrying out a full review.

whyNot.0: A rise of 20 bpm or more needs a change in practice.
whyNot.2: Concern is first reviewed and, if confirmed, CTG is advised; emergency birth is not the first step.
whyNot.3: Neither IV fluids nor facial oxygen is recommended for FHR changes in a normotensive woman.

B.q: A CTG shows repetitive variable decelerations. Pip is lying on her back and is not hypotensive. Which conservative measure is appropriate?
options: Help her change position off her back
Give her oxygen by a facial mask
Give an intravenous fluid bolus
Arrange an amnioinfusion for the baby
B.why: NG229 1.5.11: encourage her to mobilise or adopt an alternative position and avoid being supine, as position affects uterine blood flow and cord compression.

whyNot.1: Maternal facial oxygen may harm the baby and is not a conservative measure (1.5.12).
whyNot.2: IV fluids are not given for FHR abnormalities unless hypotensive or septic.
whyNot.3: Amnioinfusion is not offered for intrauterine fetal resuscitation (1.5.13).

C.q: During labour, the fetal heart rate drops to 80 bpm and stays there. No acute event is found and preparations for urgent birth are under way. When should birth be expedited if the bradycardia persists?
options: If it persists for 3 minutes
If it persists for 15 minutes
If it persists for 20 minutes
If it persists for 9 minutes
C.why: NG229 1.5.9: expedite birth if the acute bradycardia persists for 9 minutes, or less if there are significant risk factors.

whyNot.0: 3 minutes defines a prolonged deceleration, triggering urgent review, not the expedite point.
whyNot.1: 15 minutes is too long to wait.
whyNot.2: 20 minutes is far too long to wait.

C.q: Ruth's CTG: baseline risen from 130 to 150 bpm in the last hour, variability 4 bpm for 40 minutes, 4 contractions in 10, no decelerations. What is the category and action?
options: Normal: continue usual care and hourly risk checks
Suspicious: conservative measures and continue
Pathological: urgent obstetric and senior review
Normal: discuss it at the next fresh-eyes review
C.why: A 20 bpm rise in baseline and variability under 5 for 30 to 50 minutes are both amber; 2 amber features make the trace pathological (NG229 1.4.32), needing urgent obstetric and senior midwife review (1.5.7).

whyNot.0: Two features are amber, so the trace is not normal.
whyNot.1: Two amber features are pathological, not suspicious.
whyNot.3: This delays review of a pathological trace.

C.q: Continuous CTG was started for Amy because of a deceleration heard on IA. After 20 minutes the CTG is normal and she has no risk factors. What should happen?
options: Continue the CTG until the baby is born
Return to intermittent auscultation
Transfer to the obstetric unit for CTG
Repeat a 20-minute CTG every hour
C.why: NG229 1.2.13: return to IA if the CTG is normal after 20 minutes, unless the woman chooses to remain on continuous monitoring.

whyNot.0: Continuous CTG is not needed when it is normal and there are no risk factors.
whyNot.2: There is no ongoing concern requiring transfer.
whyNot.3: This is not an NG229 monitoring pattern.

reteach.title: Traffic lights for the trace
reteach.question: Think of the CTG as four traffic lights: contractions, baseline, variability and decelerations. How do the lights add up?

blocks.body: Score each of the four features white, amber or red. All white: normal. One amber: suspicious. One red, or two ambers: pathological. Then look at the woman: is she septic, is there meconium, is labour slow, is oxytocin running? The same trace means more when risk factors are present.

blocks.caption: A: normal. B: suspicious. C: pathological.

blocks.text: A single late deceleration is already a red light.

explain.body: Women at low risk of complications are offered intermittent auscultation in established labour. Continuous CTG is offered when antenatal or intrapartum risk factors exist, such as previous caesarean, meconium, pyrexia, oxytocin or an epidural.

test.q: Which woman should be offered intermittent auscultation in established labour?
options: Ali, at low risk of complications
Bea, with a previous caesarean birth
Cat, with meconium-stained liquor
Dee, on an oxytocin infusion
test.why: NG229 1.2.9: offer IA to women with a low risk of complications in established first stage.

whyNot.1: A previous caesarean is an antenatal indication for continuous CTG (1.3.2).
whyNot.2: Meconium is an intrapartum indication for continuous CTG (1.3.8).
whyNot.3: Oxytocin use is an indication for continuous CTG (1.3.8).

explain.body: Variability is the minor oscillation of the fetal heart rate, measured as the difference between the highest and lowest rate in a 1-minute segment between contractions. Normal (white) is 5 to 25 bpm.

test.q: What range of fetal heart rate variability is categorised as white (normal)?
options: 10 to 30 bpm
0 to 5 bpm
5 to 25 bpm
3 to 15 bpm
test.why: NG229 1.4.18: variability of 5 to 25 beats a minute is white.

whyNot.3: This is not the NG229 range.

explain.body: Normal: all four features white. Suspicious: any 1 amber. Pathological: any 1 red, or 2 or more amber. Use categorisation with risk factors and changes over time.

test.q: Which combination makes a CTG pathological under NICE NG229?
options: Any 1 amber feature with no red ones
3 or more amber features together
2 or more red features together
Any 1 red or 2 or more amber features
test.why: NG229 1.4.32: pathological is any 1 red feature, or 2 or more amber features.

explain.body: For women on CTG, every hourly assessment is reviewed in person by another clinician ('fresh eyes') before the next assessment. With IA, SBL v3 asks for a discussion with another midwife or doctor at least every 4 hours.

test.q: What does 'fresh eyes' mean for a woman on continuous CTG?
options: The shift leader reviews all traces at handover
An in-person hourly review by another clinician
An obstetrician reviews any pathological traces
Computer software reviews the trace every hour
test.why: NG229 1.3.6: obtain an in-person review of every hourly assessment by another clinician, completed before the next assessment (SBL v3 4.4).

whyNot.0: Fresh eyes is hourly, not at handover.
whyNot.2: Fresh eyes applies to every hourly CTG review, not just pathological traces.
whyNot.3: It is an in-person review by a clinician.
